extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers of Kantian theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and evaluating judgements of taste (what counts as 'beautiful') according to Kant: how such judgements are formed, what grounds or principles they may claim, their relation to concepts, communicability, interests, and examples/models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autonomy of Taste / a priori judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: “the subject shall judge by himself, without needing to grope about empirically among the judgements of others... his judgement should be pronounced a priori, and not be a mere imitation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine judgement of taste must be made by the subject independently (a priori) and not be mere accommodation to public opinion or imitation. Example: a young poet should not adopt the public's judgement merely for applause; later refinement of taste comes through exercise, not mere following. Distinguish 'following' (drawing on predecessors' sources) from 'imitation' (heteronomy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-cognitivity of aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: “the judgement of taste is not based upon concepts at all, and is in general not a cognitive but an aesthetical judgement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgements do not subsume an object under concepts (they are not cognitive judgements). They are responses to representations, not conclusions derived from conceptual knowledge; thus criteria that require conceptual subsumption do not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not determinable by grounds of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: “The judgement of taste is not determinable by grounds of proof, just as if it were merely subjective.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neither empirical agreement (many voices praising) nor a priori rules or expert critics can force assent to a judgement of taste. Examples: a hundred voices praising a building will not compel sincere agreement; critics' rules (Batteux, Lessing) may be rejected by one's own feeling. Anti-pattern: attempting to validate taste by adducing objective proofs or citations of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective universality (claim to universal assent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although merely subjective, a judgement of taste "claims the assent of all subjects, exactly as it would do if it were an objective judgement resting on grounds of knowledge."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A distinct feature of aesthetic judgement: it is singular (about a particular object) yet claims universal validity (I attribute this satisfaction to everyone). Evaluate whether the judgement genuinely claims this a priori universality rather than being an empirical generalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective principle / impossibility of a formula for beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no objective principle of Taste possible... we could subsume the concept of an object and thus infer by means of a syllogism that the object is beautiful. But that is absolutely impossible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not look for a universal conceptual rule or syllogistic proof that establishes beauty. Critics can analyse faculties and give examples, but cannot produce a universally applicable formula that determines beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of taste: feeling of purposiveness (free play of Imagination and Understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the judgement of taste must rest on a mere sensation of the reciprocal activity of the Imagination in its freedom and the Understanding with its conformity to law... it must therefore rest on a feeling... by the purposiveness of the representation (by which an object is given) in respect of the furtherance of the cognitive faculty in its free play.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beauty in terms of the felt harmony/purposiveness between imagination and understanding (their 'free play'), not by conformity to concepts. The 'feeling' of purposiveness is the subjective ground for the judgement of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as sensus communis / communicability of feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Taste is then the faculty of judging a priori of the communicability of feelings that are bound up with a given representation (without the mediation of a concept).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A competent judgement of taste reflects a 'sensus communis'—the capacity to abstract from private conditions and judge with regard to the possible judgements of others. Maxims to apply: (1) think for oneself; (2) put oneself in the place of every other; (3) always think consistently. Test: does the judgement consider the communicability of the feeling to others?

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of aesthetic judgement (disinterestedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the judgement of taste by which something is declared beautiful must have no interest as its determining ground.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pure aesthetic judgement is disinterested: it should not be founded on empirical inclinations or seeking personal advantage. While interest can attach indirectly (see empirical/intellectual interests), the pure judgement used to claim aesthetic validity must be free from such determining interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical interest in the Beautiful (societal/sociability interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Empirically the Beautiful interests only in society...taste as a faculty for judging everything in respect of which we can communicate our feeling to all other men.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that socially-minded (empirical) interests often attach to beauty—ornament, status, and sociability—and that these increase an object's worth by its universal communicability. When evaluating works, distinguish social/ornamental motives from pure aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual interest in natural beauty (moral affinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “to take an immediate interest in the Beauty of Nature... is always a mark of a good soul... indicates a frame of mind favourable to the moral feeling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An immediate, non-instrumental interest in natural beauty (not artifice or vanity) signals an intellectual/moral disposition; evaluate whether the interest is genuinely in natural production (deception by artificial substitutes undermines this interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples/models vs. imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Following, involving something precedent, not ‘imitation,’ is the right expression for all influence that the products of an exemplary author may have upon others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish healthy influence (examples and models that lead others to discover principles themselves) from mere imitation. Models (ancients, exemplary mathematicians, classical authors) guide development of taste but should prompt independent judgement rather than rote copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different kinds of pleasure relevant to evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures are distinct: pleasure of enjoyment (sense), moral pleasure (requires concepts and law), pleasure in the Sublime (rational contemplation + moral foundation), and pleasure in the Beautiful (pleasure of mere reflection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing aesthetic responses, identify which kind of pleasure is involved: sensory enjoyment, moral satisfaction, sublime rational pleasure, or the disinterested reflection constituting beauty. The type affects claims to universal communicability and the appropriate evaluative standard.
